analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates on loans to military families at 36 percent and outlaws loan-rollover traps.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill protecting servicemembers from 36-percent-plus interest loans drew 75 cosponsors but never got a committee vote and died.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act to bar lenders from charging active-duty troops and their families an annual interest rate above 36 percent, counting fees and renewal charges as interest. It required clear written disclosures of rates and payment obligations, barred lenders from automatically rolling over or refinancing a loan without the borrower signing new paperwork, and made knowing violations a crime. Despite 75 cosponsors from both parties, it was referred to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and died in a subcommittee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Active-duty servicemembers and their dependents, who are frequent targets of high-interest installment and payday-style loans. The bill would have capped what they can be charged at 36 percent APR including fees, forced honest disclosure of loan terms, and stopped lenders from chaining loans together through automatic rollovers. Stronger state protections would still have applied.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any creditor from charging a servicemember or dependent an annual percentage rate above 36 percent, and counts service charges, renewal charges, and fees as interest, so lenders cannot dodge the cap by relabeling costs [S2][S3].
Requires written disclosures at or before the loan is made: the APR, Truth in Lending Act disclosures, and a clear description of payment obligations [S2][S3].

Prohibits a creditor from automatically renewing, repaying, refinancing, or consolidating a servicemember's loan without new signed loan documents and fresh disclosures, targeting the rollover cycle that turns a small loan into a long-term debt trap [S2][S3].

Makes knowing violations a federal misdemeanor punishable by fine or up to a year in prison, and preserves all other legal remedies including punitive damages; stronger state protections are left in place [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-interest consumer lenders, including payday and installment lenders and other creditors whose business model depends on rates above 36 percent or on repeated loan rollovers to troops and their families. If passed, some lenders might have stopped making loans to servicemembers rather than lend at the capped rate.

drawbacks.text: A hard 36 percent rate cap can reduce access to credit for the borrowers it covers: lenders facing a capped return on small, risky loans may simply refuse to lend to servicemembers, leaving a gap for borrowers with no other options.

Enforcement runs mainly through criminal misdemeanor penalties, which is an unusual and generally weak tool for consumer credit violations; effectiveness would have depended on prosecutors rather than on a dedicated regulator or easy private lawsuits, though the bill does preserve existing remedies [S3].

The bill preempts federal and state laws inconsistent with it, which could have created confusion about how overlapping state lending rules apply, though it explicitly keeps any stronger state protections in force [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are targeted and well designed for the harm they address: a rate cap that counts fees as interest, a real anti-rollover rule, and preservation of stronger state laws. The main honest tradeoff is that some high-risk borrowers among military families might have found credit harder to get at a capped rate, and the misdemeanor-based enforcement is an odd choice for consumer lending. On balance the benefits to troops and their families outweigh these costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee in January 2005, passed to a subcommittee in April, and never came out of committee for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Graves introduced the bill on January 4, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 75 cosponsors, 41 Democrats and 34 Republicans, signaling broad bipartisan support [S4].

On April 4, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, where it sat; the full action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 109th Congress [S5].

Congress later recognized the same harm: the 2006 defense authorization bill included a Military Lending Act provision capping rates on loans to servicemembers at 36 percent, showing the underlying problem was real and legislatively addressable.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-rate consumer lenders, including payday and installment lenders serving military communities, stayed free to charge troops and their families above-36-percent rates and to roll over loans for the remainder of the Congress. Servicemembers did get some protection shortly after through a 2006 military lending provision, but this bill itself died quietly in committee despite bipartisan backing.

for.name: Rep. Sam Graves
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it before the House.

for.name: 75 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support across the House.

against.name: House Committee on Veterans' Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in January 2005 and never reported it out; it went to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity in April and got no further action [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action; as majority, House Republicans controlled what reached the floor, and no vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan, with 41 Democratic and 34 Republican cosponsors; there was never a vote, so the opposition that buried it never had to register a public position [S4].

industries.note: A 36 percent APR cap that counts fees and renewal charges as interest, plus a ban on automatic rollovers, strikes directly at the rollover-driven revenue model these lenders use with military borrowers. Because the bill died, they kept charging troops above-cap rates through the rest of the Congress [S2][S3].

Most conventional consumer lenders charge well under 36 percent and would have faced mainly new disclosure paperwork; lenders near the cap, including some credit card and subprime installment lenders, would have lost pricing flexibility on loans to servicemembers [S2][S3].
